# Finance and Corporate Policy {#finance}

In 1976 a small fund company in Pennsylvania launched a mutual fund that promised
never to beat the market. It would simply hold the stocks in the S&P 500 in
proportion to their market value and charge very little for doing so. The offering
raised far less than its sponsors had hoped, and many in the industry regarded
it as a curiosity. Half a century later, index funds are among the largest pools of
capital in the world, and the firm that launched that first retail index fund,
Vanguard, is one of the largest asset managers anywhere. Why would investors
deliberately give up the chance to outperform? Why do cash-rich companies borrow
billions of dollars they do not seem to need? Why did a hedge fund whose partners
included two Nobel laureates nearly collapse in 1998, and why did the shares of a struggling
video-game retailer rise more than tenfold in a few weeks of January 2021?

Each puzzle sits on a different branch of financial theory, but they share a root.
Finance studies how people and firms trade claims on uncertain future cash flows,
and almost every theory in the field is an answer to one of three questions.
**How should risk be priced?** ([portfolio theory](#portfolio-theory) and the capital asset pricing
model). **How much do prices reveal?** (the [efficient market hypothesis](#efficient-market-hypothesis), the limits
to arbitrage, and behavioural finance). **How should a firm finance itself and
what should it do with its cash?** (the [Modigliani-Miller theorems](#modigliani-miller), the trade-off
and [pecking order](#trade-off-pecking-order) theories, and [free cash flow theory](#free-cash-flow)). This chapter develops all
eight, with formal logic where it is standard and applications to investing and
corporate policy. They build on [Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)),
[Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)), and
[Signaling theory](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)), and the behavioural theories connect to
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory-model) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-model)) and
[Heuristics and biases](#heuristics-biases) (Section \@ref(heuristics-biases)) (Table \@ref(tab:tab-fin-glance)).

```{r tab-fin-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "[Portfolio theory](#portfolio-theory)", "How should an investor combine risky assets?", "Investor / portfolio", "Markowitz (1952)",
  "[Capital asset pricing model](#capm)", "Which risks earn a premium in equilibrium?", "Asset / market", "Sharpe (1964), Lintner (1965)",
  "[Efficient market hypothesis](#efficient-market-hypothesis)", "How fully do prices reflect available information?", "Market", "Fama (1970)",
  "[Modigliani-Miller theorems](#modigliani-miller)", "When does financing affect firm value?", "Firm / market", "Modigliani & Miller (1958, 1963)",
  "[Trade-off and pecking order](#trade-off-pecking-order)", "Why do firms choose the leverage they do?", "Firm", "Kraus & Litzenberger (1973), Myers (1984)",
  "[Free cash flow theory](#free-cash-flow)", "Why can surplus cash destroy value?", "Firm / manager", "Jensen (1986)",
  "[Limits to arbitrage](#limits-to-arbitrage)", "Why can mispricing persist?", "Arbitrageur / market", "Shleifer & Vishny (1997)",
  "[Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance)", "How do investor psychology and sentiment shape prices?", "Investor / market", "Barberis & Thaler (2003)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: theories of finance and corporate policy.")
```

## Portfolio Theory {#portfolio-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Investors should evaluate an asset not by its own risk but by its
contribution to the risk of the whole portfolio. Combining assets whose returns are
imperfectly correlated reduces risk without sacrificing expected return, and
rational investors choose among portfolios on the **efficient frontier**.

**Origins.** Economics and finance. @markowitz1952 formulated mean-variance
portfolio selection. @tobin1958 added the separation theorem. Markowitz shared the
1990 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Merton Miller and William
Sharpe.

**Level of analysis.** Individual investor or institutional portfolio.

**Key constructs.** Expected return, variance, covariance, correlation,
diversification, efficient frontier, global minimum-variance portfolio, tangency
portfolio, Sharpe ratio.

**Boundary conditions.** Investors care only about the mean and variance of
portfolio returns (returns are approximately normal or utility is quadratic),
inputs are known or well estimated, and the investment horizon is a single period.

**Related theories.** [CAPM](#capm), [Myopic loss aversion](#myopic-loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(myopic-loss-aversion)),
[Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)), [Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Before 1952, investment advice focused on picking good securities: identify the
asset with the highest expected value and buy it. @markowitz1952 observed that this
rule cannot explain why prudent investors hold many securities rather than one.
Diversification is rational only if investors also care about risk, and once they
do, the right unit of analysis is the portfolio. Markowitz measured risk as the
**variance** of portfolio returns, which depends on the **covariances** among assets.
@tobin1958 then showed that with a riskless asset, every investor should hold the
same risky portfolio and adjust overall risk by mixing it with the riskless asset.
This **separation theorem** bridged portfolio choice and equilibrium asset pricing.

### Core logic and propositions

For a portfolio with weights $w_i$ on $N$ assets, expected return is a weighted
average, but variance is not:

$$E[R_p] = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, E[R_i], \qquad
\sigma_p^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_i w_j \sigma_{ij}.$$

With two assets the variance becomes
$\sigma_p^2 = w^2 \sigma_1^2 + (1-w)^2 \sigma_2^2 + 2w(1-w)\rho_{12}\sigma_1\sigma_2$.
Whenever the correlation $\rho_{12}$ is below one, the portfolio's standard deviation
is less than the weighted average of the two standard deviations. That gap is the
gain from diversification. For an equally weighted portfolio of $N$ assets with
average variance $\bar{\sigma}^2$ and average covariance $\overline{\text{cov}}$,

$$\sigma_p^2 = \frac{1}{N}\,\bar{\sigma}^2 + \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right)\overline{\text{cov}}.$$

As $N$ grows, the first term vanishes but the second does not. Risk that is specific
to individual assets (**idiosyncratic** risk) can be diversified away. Risk that
assets share (**systematic** risk) cannot. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-diversify)
plots this decomposition.

```{r fig-fin-diversify, fig.cap = "Illustrative diversification curve for an equally weighted portfolio. Each stock has 30 percent volatility and pairwise correlation 0.25. Idiosyncratic risk falls quickly as stocks are added, but systematic risk sets a floor.", fig.height = 3.8}
avg_var <- 0.30^2
avg_cov <- 0.25 * avg_var
div <- tibble::tibble(n = 1:50) |>
  mutate(sd_p = sqrt(avg_var / n + (1 - 1 / n) * avg_cov))
floor_sd <- sqrt(avg_cov)
ggplot(div, aes(n, sd_p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = floor_sd, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = floor_sd - 0.012, label = "Systematic risk (cannot be diversified)",
           size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 0.23, label = "Idiosyncratic risk\nfalls with more holdings",
           size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.12, 0.31)) +
  labs(x = "Number of stocks in the portfolio", y = "Portfolio standard deviation",
       title = "Diversification removes only part of the risk",
       caption = "Illustrative: sd = sqrt(var / N + (1 - 1/N) x cov), volatility 30 percent, correlation 0.25.")
```

The theory's central propositions can be stated as follows.

- **P1 (Risk is a portfolio property).** The risk an asset adds to a portfolio depends
  on its covariance with the other holdings, not on its stand-alone variance.
- **P2 (Diversification).** Combining imperfectly correlated assets lowers portfolio
  variance for a given expected return. Only systematic risk remains in a large,
  well-diversified portfolio.
- **P3 (Efficiency).** A rational mean-variance investor holds a portfolio on the
  upper boundary of the feasible set: no other portfolio offers a higher expected
  return for the same variance.
- **P4 (Separation).** With a riskless asset, every mean-variance investor holds the
  same risky portfolio, the **tangency portfolio** with the highest Sharpe ratio
  $(E[R_p] - r_f)/\sigma_p$, and expresses risk tolerance only through the share
  invested in it [@tobin1958].

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-frontier) builds the frontier from five simulated asset
classes. The blue curve is the mean-variance frontier, whose upper arm is the
efficient frontier. The orange **capital allocation line** runs from the riskless
rate to the tangency portfolio and dominates every other point on the frontier.

```{r fig-fin-frontier, fig.cap = "Illustrative efficient frontier for five simulated asset classes. Grey points are random long-only portfolios, the blue curve is the mean-variance frontier (short sales allowed), and the orange line combines the riskless asset with the tangency portfolio.", fig.height = 4.6}
set.seed(1952)
assets <- c("Bonds", "Large caps", "Small caps", "International", "Real estate")
mu  <- c(0.035, 0.070, 0.090, 0.075, 0.065)
sdv <- c(0.06, 0.16, 0.24, 0.19, 0.20)
R <- matrix(c(1, .10, .05, .10, .20,
              .10, 1, .80, .65, .55,
              .05, .80, 1, .60, .50,
              .10, .65, .60, 1, .50,
              .20, .55, .50, .50, 1), 5)
Sigma <- diag(sdv) %*% R %*% diag(sdv)
Si <- solve(Sigma)
one <- rep(1, 5)
A <- drop(t(one) %*% Si %*% mu)
B <- drop(t(mu) %*% Si %*% mu)
C <- drop(t(one) %*% Si %*% one)
D <- B * C - A^2
frontier <- tibble::tibble(m = seq(0.02, 0.105, length.out = 300)) |>
  mutate(s = sqrt((C * m^2 - 2 * A * m + B) / D),
         arm = ifelse(m >= A / C, "Efficient", "Inefficient"))
rf <- 0.02
w_t <- drop(Si %*% (mu - rf))
w_t <- w_t / sum(w_t)
mu_t <- sum(w_t * mu)
sd_t <- sqrt(drop(t(w_t) %*% Sigma %*% w_t))
cml <- tibble::tibble(s = c(0, 0.20)) |> mutate(m = rf + (mu_t - rf) / sd_t * s)
rand <- replicate(3000, {
  w <- rexp(5)^2
  w <- w / sum(w)
  c(sum(w * mu), sqrt(drop(t(w) %*% Sigma %*% w)))
})
rand <- tibble::tibble(m = rand[1, ], s = rand[2, ])
pts <- tibble::tibble(asset = assets, m = mu, s = sdv)
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = rand, aes(s, m), colour = ink[["grid"]], size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = filter(frontier, arm == "Inefficient"), aes(s, m), colour = pal[["blue"]],
            linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_path(data = filter(frontier, arm == "Efficient"), aes(s, m), colour = pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_line(data = cml, aes(s, m), colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(s, m), colour = pal[["aqua"]], size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(data = pts, aes(s, m, label = asset), nudge_x = 0.006, hjust = 0, size = 3.1,
            colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("point", x = sd_t, y = mu_t, colour = ink[["primary"]], size = 3.2, shape = 21,
           fill = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = sd_t - 0.005, y = mu_t + 0.006, label = "Tangency portfolio", hjust = 1,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.003, y = rf - 0.004, label = "Riskless rate", hjust = 0, size = 3.1,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.01, 0.105)) +
  labs(x = "Standard deviation of annual return", y = "Expected annual return",
       title = "The efficient frontier and the capital allocation line",
       caption = "Illustrative: simulated asset classes with assumed means, volatilities, and correlations. Riskless rate = 2 percent.")
```

The lowest point on the frontier, the **global minimum-variance portfolio**, has a
closed-form solution that requires no estimate of expected returns at all:
$w_{\text{GMV}} = \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1} / (\mathbf{1}'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1})$, where
$\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix. The short computation below applies it to three
illustrative asset classes.

```{r fin-minvar, echo = TRUE}
# Illustrative covariance matrix of annual returns (volatility 6, 16, 24 percent)
Sigma3 <- matrix(c(0.0036, 0.0019, 0.0029,
                   0.0019, 0.0256, 0.0243,
                   0.0029, 0.0243, 0.0576),
                 nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
                 dimnames = list(c("Bonds", "Large caps", "Small caps"),
                                 c("Bonds", "Large caps", "Small caps")))
x <- solve(Sigma3, rep(1, 3))                # inverse(Sigma) times a vector of ones
w_gmv <- x / sum(x)                          # normalise so the weights sum to one
round(w_gmv, 3)
sqrt(drop(t(w_gmv) %*% Sigma3 %*% w_gmv))    # volatility of the minimum-variance portfolio
```

The solution puts about 93 percent in bonds, a small long position in large caps,
and a small short position in small caps. Its volatility is slightly *below* that of
bonds alone, even though every other asset is riskier than bonds. That is
Markowitz's insight in miniature: a risky asset can lower portfolio risk when its
correlation with the rest of the portfolio is low enough.

### Evidence and extensions

Portfolio theory is normative, so its evidence concerns whether its prescriptions
work. The gains from diversification are real and large, but the optimiser is very
sensitive to its inputs: it loads heavily on the assets whose expected returns are
most overestimated. @demiguel2009 compared
fourteen optimised strategies with a naive rule that puts $1/N$ in each asset and
found that none consistently beat the naive rule out of sample across the datasets
they studied, because estimation error offset the theoretical gains.

::: {.debate}
**Is variance the right measure of risk?** Mean-variance analysis treats upside and
downside deviations symmetrically and assumes that the first two moments capture
everything investors care about. Real return distributions have fat tails, and
correlations tend to rise in crises, which is exactly when diversification is most
needed. Behavioural evidence adds that investors weigh losses more heavily than
gains [@kahneman1979; @barberis2013], see [Loss aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)). The
pragmatic response has been shrinkage estimators, factor risk models, and weight
constraints, which keep Markowitz's architecture while taming its sensitivity to
inputs.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Concentration in employer stock: the Enron 401(k) accounts.** The clearest
violation of portfolio theory in household finance is holding a large share of
retirement savings in one's own employer, whose wages and stock share the same
firm-specific risk. When Enron filed for bankruptcy in December 2001, many employees
whose 401(k) accounts were heavily invested in company stock lost much of their
retirement savings along with their jobs. The episode fed into later US reforms that
gave plan participants the right to diversify out of employer stock.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Households with lower financial literacy hold less diversified portfolios,
  measured by the share of idiosyncratic variance in portfolio variance.
- *H2.* Employees hold more employer stock when the employer has recently
  outperformed (extrapolation), controlling for plan design.

**Measures.** Portfolio variance decomposition, number of effective holdings
(inverse Herfindahl of weights), Sharpe ratio, tracking error, out-of-sample
volatility.

**Designs and data.** Out-of-sample backtests with rolling estimation windows,
household brokerage and pension records, administrative data on retirement plans,
natural experiments from changes in default investment options.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating historical averages as expected returns.** Plugging sample means into an
optimiser produces portfolios that are extremely concentrated and unstable, because
the optimiser chases estimation noise. Report out-of-sample performance, use
shrinkage or factor models for inputs, and compare against the naive $1/N$ and
minimum-variance benchmarks before claiming that an optimised portfolio adds value.
:::

## Capital Asset Pricing Model {#capm}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** In equilibrium, an asset's expected return depends only on its
**beta**, its sensitivity to the return on the market portfolio. Idiosyncratic risk
earns no premium because investors can diversify it away.

**Origins.** Finance. @sharpe1964 and @lintner1965, building on @markowitz1952 and
@tobin1958. Extended to multifactor models by @fama1992 and @fama1993.

**Level of analysis.** Individual asset within a market in equilibrium.

**Key constructs.** Market portfolio, beta, market risk premium, security market
line, alpha, systematic versus idiosyncratic risk, factor premia.

**Boundary conditions.** Investors are mean-variance optimisers with common beliefs,
can borrow and lend at the riskless rate, face no taxes or transaction costs, and
hold the market portfolio of all risky assets.

**Related theories.** [Portfolio theory](#portfolio-theory),
[Efficient market hypothesis](#efficient-market-hypothesis),
[Modigliani-Miller](#modigliani-miller), [Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

If every investor follows Markowitz and Tobin and all share the same beliefs, they
all hold the same tangency portfolio. In equilibrium, that portfolio must be the
**market portfolio**, because the supply of every asset must be held by someone.
@sharpe1964 and @lintner1965 worked out the pricing implication independently,
and related versions were developed by Jack Treynor and Jan Mossin. The result was
the first general equilibrium model of risk and return, and it gave both investors
and corporate managers a usable formula for the cost of capital.

### Core logic and propositions

The CAPM states that the expected excess return on any asset is proportional to its
beta:

$$E[R_i] = r_f + \beta_i \left( E[R_m] - r_f \right), \qquad
\beta_i = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(R_i, R_m)}{\operatorname{Var}(R_m)}.$$

An investor who holds the market portfolio cares about how a new asset changes the
risk of that portfolio, which depends on the asset's covariance with the market. An
asset that falls when the market falls must offer a higher expected return. Purely
idiosyncratic risk adds almost nothing and earns only the riskless rate.

- **P1 (Only systematic risk is priced).** Idiosyncratic volatility should not predict
  expected returns.
- **P2 (Linearity).** Expected returns are linear in beta, with intercept $r_f$ and
  slope equal to the market risk premium.
- **P3 (Zero alpha).** In equilibrium the intercept $\alpha_i$ in the regression of
  excess asset returns on excess market returns is zero for every asset.
- **P4 (Market efficiency of the market portfolio).** The market portfolio is
  mean-variance efficient. The [CAPM](#capm) is equivalent to this statement [@roll1977].

### Mechanism

The **security market line** (SML) in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-sml) is the CAPM's
testable prediction. Assets above the line (positive alpha) would be bid up and
assets below it sold until both return to the line. The orange points illustrate the
pattern that empirical tests have repeatedly found: a line that is **too flat**,
with low-beta portfolios earning more and high-beta portfolios earning less than
the CAPM predicts [@fama2004].

```{r fig-fin-sml, fig.cap = "Stylised security market line. The blue line is the CAPM prediction. Orange points are stylised beta-sorted portfolios lying on a flatter line, the pattern reported in many empirical tests of the CAPM. Not empirical data.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1964)
rf_s <- 0.03
mrp <- 0.06
sml <- tibble::tibble(beta = seq(0, 2, by = 0.01)) |> mutate(er = rf_s + beta * mrp)
deciles <- tibble::tibble(beta = seq(0.5, 1.7, length.out = 10)) |>
  mutate(er = 0.062 + 0.022 * beta + rnorm(10, 0, 0.003))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = sml, aes(beta, er), colour = pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(data = deciles, aes(beta, er), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = pal[["orange"]],
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8, fullrange = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = deciles, aes(beta, er), colour = pal[["orange"]], size = 2.6) +
  annotate("point", x = 1, y = rf_s + mrp, size = 3.4, shape = 21, fill = pal[["blue"]],
           colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.97, y = rf_s + mrp + 0.007, label = "Market portfolio (beta = 1)", hjust = 1,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.05, y = 0.135, label = "Above the line: positive alpha", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.95, y = 0.04, label = "Below the line: negative alpha", hjust = 1,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.75, y = 0.152, label = "CAPM security\nmarket line", hjust = 0.5,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.72, y = 0.083, label = "Stylised empirical\nrelation (flatter)", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.02, 0.16)) +
  labs(x = "Beta", y = "Expected annual return",
       title = "The security market line in theory and in tests",
       caption = "Stylised: riskless rate 3 percent, market risk premium 6 percent. Points are simulated, not estimated.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

Early tests in the late 1960s and 1970s found that average returns rose with beta,
but less steeply than the model predicts. @roll1977 argued that the CAPM is not
testable in practice, because the true market portfolio includes every risky asset
and no index measures it. The decisive challenge came from @fama1992: for US stocks
from 1963 to 1990, beta had little power to explain average returns once firm size
and the book-to-market ratio were included. Small firms and "value" firms with high
book-to-market ratios earned more than their betas implied. @fama1993 responded with a three-factor model in which
returns load on the market, a size factor (SMB, small minus big), and a value factor
(HML, high minus low book-to-market):

$$R_i - r_f = \alpha_i + b_i (R_m - r_f) + s_i \, \text{SMB} + h_i \, \text{HML} + \varepsilon_i .$$

@jegadeesh1993 documented **momentum**, the tendency of recent winners to keep
outperforming recent losers over three to twelve months, which the three-factor model
does not explain. @carhart1997 added a momentum factor for fund evaluation, and
@fama2015 added profitability and investment factors. Table
\@ref(tab:tab-fin-factors) compares the main models.

```{r tab-fin-factors}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Risk factors`, ~`What it explains`, ~`Main limitation`,
  "CAPM (Sharpe 1964, Lintner 1965)", "Market excess return", "Why diversifiable risk is not rewarded", "Flat empirical SML, size and value anomalies",
  "Three-factor (Fama & French 1993)", "Market, size (SMB), value (HML)", "Size and value premia", "Momentum, profitability",
  "Four-factor (Carhart 1997)", "Three factors plus momentum", "Persistence in fund returns", "Factors are empirical, not derived from theory",
  "Five-factor (Fama & French 2015)", "Market, size, value, profitability, investment", "Profitability and investment patterns", "Momentum, low-beta anomaly, short-term reversals"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "From the CAPM to multifactor models of expected returns.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Risk, mispricing, or data mining?** The size and value premia admit two readings.
In the risk reading, small and value firms are exposed to distress or business-cycle
risk that the market beta misses, so their premia are rational compensation. In the
behavioural reading, investors extrapolate past growth and overprice glamour firms,
so the premia reflect correctable mispricing [@barberis2003]. A third concern is
statistical. @harvey2016 counted hundreds of proposed return factors and argued that,
given the number of researchers searching the same data, a new factor should clear a
t-statistic hurdle of about 3.0 rather than the conventional 2.0. The CAPM survives
because it is simple and coherent, but few researchers regard it as an adequate
empirical description of the cross-section of returns [@fama2004].
:::

### Applications in business

In a large survey of chief financial officers, @graham2001 found that the CAPM was
the most popular method for estimating the cost of equity, used by roughly three in
four respondents. Investment managers use CAPM or multifactor alpha as the standard
measure of skill, a practice that began with @jensen1968.

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: divisional hurdle rates.** A diversified company has a
regulated utility division and a biotechnology division and uses one company-wide
cost of capital of 9 percent for all projects. Suppose the utility division's asset
beta is about 0.4 and the biotechnology division's is about 1.5. With a riskless
rate of 3 percent and a market risk premium of 6 percent, the CAPM implies hurdle
rates of roughly 5.4 and 12 percent. The single company rate rejects good low-risk
utility projects and accepts bad high-risk biotechnology projects. The remedy is
divisional hurdle rates based on betas of comparable pure-play firms: the cost of
capital belongs to the project, not the firm.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* After controlling for market beta, firms with higher customer satisfaction
  earn lower subsequent returns because their cash flows are less risky.
- *H2.* The alpha of an investment strategy based on a new signal is not explained by
  the Fama-French five factors plus momentum.

**Designs.** Time-series regressions of portfolio excess returns on factors (alpha
tests), Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of returns on characteristics and
betas, portfolio sorts with out-of-sample periods.

**Data.** CRSP and Compustat for US equities, factor returns from Kenneth French's
data library, international equity databases, mutual fund return databases.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Mistaking a factor loading for an explanation.** Showing that a strategy's returns
load on a factor does not explain *why* the factor earns a premium. Equally, an
anomaly that disappears after controlling for factors may simply have been absorbed
by a factor that is itself an unexplained anomaly. State whether a variable is meant
to proxy for risk or for mispricing, and design a test that can tell the two apart.
:::

## Efficient Market Hypothesis {#efficient-market-hypothesis}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** In an efficient market, prices fully reflect available information,
so no investor can earn returns in excess of fair compensation for risk by trading on
that information.

**Origins.** Finance. @fama1970 synthesised the theory and evidence, building on the
random-walk literature. Fama shared the 2013 Nobel Memorial Prize with Lars Peter
Hansen and Robert Shiller, one of the hypothesis's leading critics.

**Level of analysis.** Market.

**Key constructs.** Information set, weak, semi-strong, and strong form efficiency,
abnormal return, joint hypothesis problem, event study, anomaly.

**Boundary conditions.** Information is widely available, trading costs are low,
and enough well-capitalised investors trade on information to keep prices close to
fundamental value.

**Related theories.** [Limits to arbitrage](#limits-to-arbitrage),
[Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance),
[Wisdom of the crowd](#wisdom-of-the-crowd) (Section \@ref(wisdom-of-the-crowd)),
[Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Statisticians had long noticed that stock price changes look like a random walk. The
insight behind the EMH is that this is what a well-functioning market should
produce: if prices already reflect all
predictable information, only *new* information moves them, and new information is
by definition unpredictable. @fama1970 organised the evidence around three
information sets, summarised in Table \@ref(tab:tab-fin-emh-forms).

```{r tab-fin-emh-forms}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Form, ~`Information reflected in prices`, ~`Implication if true`, ~`Typical test`,
  "Weak form", "Past prices and trading volume", "Technical analysis cannot earn abnormal returns", "Return autocorrelation, trading-rule backtests",
  "Semi-strong form", "All publicly available information", "Fundamental analysis of public data cannot earn abnormal returns", "Event studies of announcements",
  "Strong form", "All information, including private", "Even insiders cannot profit", "Returns to insider trades and professional managers"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The three forms of market efficiency (following Fama, 1970).")
```

### Core logic and propositions

Formally, a market is efficient with respect to an information set $\Phi_t$ if the
expected return conditional on that information equals the equilibrium expected
return implied by some model of risk:

$$E\left[ R_{i,t+1} \mid \Phi_t \right] = E^{*}\left[ R_{i,t+1} \right], \qquad
\text{so that} \quad E\left[ R_{i,t+1} - E^{*}[R_{i,t+1}] \mid \Phi_t \right] = 0 .$$

The abnormal return, the gap between realised and model-implied returns, should be
unpredictable using $\Phi_t$. This formulation exposes the **joint hypothesis
problem**: every test of efficiency is also a test of the asset pricing model that
defines $E^{*}$. If returns appear predictable, either the market is inefficient or
the risk model is wrong, and the data alone cannot say which [@fama1970; @fama1998].

- **P1 (No predictable abnormal returns).** Abnormal returns are unpredictable from
  information in the relevant set.
- **P2 (Rapid and unbiased adjustment).** Prices react to new public information
  quickly and, on average, by the right amount, with no systematic drift or reversal.
- **P3 (No persistent skill).** Professional investors do not outperform
  risk-adjusted benchmarks after costs on a persistent basis.

### Mechanism

The EMH rests on competition among informed traders, who trade until the price no
longer offers a profit. @grossman1980 showed that if prices fully reflected all information, no
one would have an incentive to pay for information, because they could learn it for
free from prices. Yet if no one gathered information, prices could not reflect it. The
resolution is an equilibrium degree of *inefficiency*: prices must be noisy enough
to compensate informed traders for their costs. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-emh-loop)
shows this loop.

```{r fig-fin-emh-loop, fig.cap = "Mechanism of informational efficiency and the Grossman-Stiglitz paradox. Informed trading makes prices informative, which lowers the profit from becoming informed. In equilibrium, noise keeps prices informative but imperfect, so information gathering remains just worth its cost."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  N [label = "New information\\n(earnings, macro news)", %s]
  I [label = "Informed traders\\nacquire information\\n(costly)", %s]
  T [label = "Trading on\\nmispricing", %s]
  P [label = "Prices reflect\\ninformation", %s]
  G [label = "Profit from being\\ninformed falls", %s]
  Z [label = "Noise trading\\nand cost of\\ninformation", %s]
  N -> I -> T -> P
  P -> G
  G -> I [label = " fewer informed\\n traders", style = dashed, constraint = false]
  Z -> G [style = dashed, arrowhead = tee]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

**Event studies**, which measure abnormal returns around announcements, show that
prices typically react within minutes to earnings, merger bids, and macroeconomic
releases, consistent with P2. On P3, @jensen1968 and @carhart1997 found that mutual
funds on average do not beat risk-adjusted benchmarks after fees, and that the
persistence that exists is concentrated among the worst performers.

Against this, researchers have catalogued **anomalies**. The best documented is
**post-earnings-announcement drift** (PEAD): after a large positive earnings surprise,
returns continue to drift upward for weeks, and after a large negative surprise they
drift downward. @bernard1989 showed that the drift is difficult to explain as compensation for
risk and concluded that it reflects a delayed price response, as if investors
fail to incorporate the full implications of earnings news. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-pead)
sketches the pattern.

```{r fig-fin-pead, fig.cap = "Stylised post-earnings-announcement drift. Cumulative abnormal returns jump at the announcement and then continue to drift in the direction of the surprise for about two months, a pattern inconsistent with complete and immediate adjustment. Not empirical data.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1989)
days <- -10:60
drift <- function(t) ifelse(t < 0, 0, (1 - exp(-t / 25)) / (1 - exp(-60 / 25)))
pead <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(day = days, car = ifelse(days < 0, 0.0004 * (days + 10), 0.004 + 0.025 + 0.022 * drift(days)),
                 group = "Largest positive surprises"),
  tibble::tibble(day = days, car = 0,
                 group = "Small surprises"),
  tibble::tibble(day = days, car = ifelse(days < 0, -0.0004 * (days + 10), -0.004 - 0.025 - 0.025 * drift(days)),
                 group = "Largest negative surprises")
) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(car = car + cumsum(rnorm(n(), 0, 0.0007))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("Largest positive surprises", "Small surprises", "Largest negative surprises")))
ggplot(pead, aes(day, car, colour = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["grid"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 0.062, label = "Announcement day", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 35, y = 0.035, label = "Drift continues\nafter the news", hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal[c("blue", "aqua", "orange")])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Trading days relative to the earnings announcement", y = "Cumulative abnormal return",
       colour = NULL, title = "Prices underreact to earnings news",
       caption = "Stylised pattern consistent with Bernard and Thomas (1989). Simulated paths, not estimates.")
```

A second line of evidence concerns the *level* of prices rather than the predictability
of returns. If a stock's price is the expected present value of its future dividends,
then the price $p_t$ is a forecast of the ex post rational price
$p_t^{*} = \sum_{k \ge 1} D_{t+k}/(1+r)^k$. A rational forecast must be less volatile
than the quantity it forecasts, so $\operatorname{Var}(p_t) \le \operatorname{Var}(p_t^{*})$.
@shiller1981 found that US stock prices were far more volatile than this
bound allowed, a result he interpreted as evidence that prices move too much to be
justified by news about fundamentals.

::: {.debate}
**Is the market efficient?** The debate has matured rather than ended. Defenders
emphasise that most anomalies are small, fragile, or explained by risk, that
apparent overreactions are about as common as underreactions, and that active
managers as a group do not beat passive benchmarks after costs
[@fama1998; @malkiel2003]. Critics reply that excess volatility, bubbles, and
persistent anomalies show that prices can deviate from fundamental value for long
periods [@shiller1981; @shleifer2000]. A middle ground comes from @mclean2016: the
returns to 97 published anomalies were about 26 percent lower out of sample and about
58 percent lower after publication. Some predictability was statistical bias, but
much was real mispricing that informed traders then arbitraged away, as Grossman and
Stiglitz would predict. The joint 2013 Nobel prize to Fama and Shiller captures the
state of the field: markets are hard to beat, but prices are not always right.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Index funds and the rise of Vanguard.** The most consequential application of the
EMH is the index fund. @samuelson1974 argued that few managers could be expected to
beat the market and called for a low-cost fund that simply tracked a broad index.
In 1976 John Bogle's newly founded Vanguard launched the First Index Investment Trust, later renamed the Vanguard 500
Index Fund, to track the S&P 500. The initial offering raised only a small fraction
of its target. @sharpe1991 later stated the logic with great economy: before costs,
the average actively managed dollar must earn the market return, so after costs it
must underperform the average passive dollar. The argument requires only that
outperformance be zero-sum before costs. @french2008 estimated that over
1980-2006 US investors spent about two thirds of one percent of the aggregate value
of the market each year on fees, trading costs, and other expenses of active
investing. Vanguard's structure reinforced the strategy: the company is owned by its
funds, and through them by fund shareholders, which aligns its incentives with low
costs. The later growth of passive investing raises a new question: do markets
remain informationally efficient if fewer investors gather information? That is the
Grossman-Stiglitz paradox in practical form.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Post-earnings-announcement drift is stronger for firms with lower investor
  attention (fewer analysts, announcements on Fridays or busy news days).
- *H2.* Anomaly returns decline after the publication of the academic paper that
  documents them, and the decline is larger for anomalies that are cheaper to trade.

**Designs.** Event studies with market-model or factor-model abnormal returns,
calendar-time portfolio regressions, difference-in-differences around changes in
information access, tests of return predictability with out-of-sample validation.

**Data.** CRSP daily returns, I/B/E/S analyst forecasts and earnings surprises,
news timestamps, SEC EDGAR filings.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Confusing "no free lunch" with "prices are right".** The EMH predicts that abnormal
returns are unpredictable, not that prices equal fundamental value at every moment.
A market can be hard to beat and still be wrong, because mispricing may be
unpredictable in timing or too risky to correct. Conversely, finding a predictable
return pattern does not prove inefficiency until risk and trading costs are ruled out.
Always state the asset pricing model your test assumes.
:::

## The Modigliani-Miller Theorems {#modigliani-miller}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** In a perfect capital market, a firm's value is determined by its
real assets and investment policy, not by how it is financed. Capital structure and
dividend policy are irrelevant. Once corporate taxes are introduced, debt adds value
through the interest tax shield.

**Origins.** Economics and finance. @modigliani1958 on capital structure,
@miller1961 on dividend policy, and @modigliani1963 on corporate taxes. Modigliani
received the Nobel Memorial Prize in 1985 and Miller in 1990.

**Level of analysis.** Firm in a capital market.

**Key constructs.** Firm value, leverage, cost of equity, cost of debt, weighted
average cost of capital (WACC), homemade leverage, arbitrage, interest tax shield.

**Boundary conditions.** No taxes, bankruptcy costs, transaction costs, or information
asymmetries, investors can borrow on the same terms as firms, and investment policy
is held fixed.

**Related theories.** [Trade-off and pecking order](#trade-off-pecking-order),
[Free cash flow theory](#free-cash-flow), [Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)),
[Signaling theory](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Before 1958, corporate finance was largely descriptive and institutional, and
practitioners believed that a judicious amount of cheap debt lowered a firm's cost
of capital. @modigliani1958 showed that this belief rests on an error. If investors
can borrow and lend on the same terms as firms, any leverage a firm chooses can be
undone or replicated by investors on their own account (**homemade leverage**). Two
firms with identical assets but different capital structures must then have the same
total value, or investors could earn a riskless profit by selling the overvalued firm
and buying the undervalued one. The proof by arbitrage was itself a methodological
innovation and became the template for modern asset pricing, including option
pricing.

### Core logic and propositions

The results are usually stated as three propositions and a tax correction. Let $V_L$
and $V_U$ be the values of levered and unlevered firms with the same assets, $D$ and
$E$ the market values of debt and equity, $r_A$ the return on assets, and $r_D$ and
$r_E$ the returns on debt and equity.

- **Proposition I (Value irrelevance).** $V_L = V_U$. The value of the firm is
  independent of its capital structure.
- **Proposition II (Cost of equity).** The expected return on equity rises linearly
  with the debt-to-equity ratio, exactly offsetting the apparent gain from cheaper debt:

$$r_E = r_A + \frac{D}{E}\left( r_A - r_D \right), \qquad
\text{WACC} = \frac{E}{V} r_E + \frac{D}{V} r_D = r_A .$$

- **Proposition III (Dividend irrelevance).** Holding investment fixed, the split of
  earnings between dividends and retention does not affect value, because a dividend
  financed by issuing new shares transfers value from old to new shareholders one for
  one [@miller1961].
- **Tax correction.** With a corporate tax rate $\tau_c$ and permanent debt, interest
  payments are deductible and

$$V_L = V_U + \tau_c D, \qquad \text{WACC}_{\text{after-tax}} = r_A \left( 1 - \tau_c \frac{D}{V} \right),$$

  so value rises with leverage [@modigliani1963].

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-mm) shows the propositions graphically. Without taxes,
substituting cheap debt for expensive equity leaves the WACC unchanged because equity
holders demand a higher return for the extra financial risk (in CAPM terms, leverage
raises the equity beta). With taxes, the WACC falls as leverage rises.

```{r fig-fin-mm, fig.cap = "Illustrative Modigliani-Miller propositions. Without taxes, the cost of equity rises with leverage and the weighted average cost of capital stays flat. With a 25 percent corporate tax, the after-tax WACC declines as leverage rises because of the interest tax shield.", fig.height = 4.2}
rA <- 0.10
rD <- 0.05
tc <- 0.25
mm <- tidyr::expand_grid(L = seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.01),
                         regime = c("No taxes (1958)", "Corporate tax of 25 percent (1963)")) |>
  mutate(DE = L / (1 - L),
         `Cost of equity` = ifelse(regime == "No taxes (1958)", rA + DE * (rA - rD),
                                   rA + DE * (1 - tc) * (rA - rD)),
         `Cost of debt` = ifelse(regime == "No taxes (1958)", rD, rD * (1 - tc)),
         WACC = ifelse(regime == "No taxes (1958)", rA, rA * (1 - tc * L))) |>
  select(-DE) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Cost of equity`, `Cost of debt`, WACC), names_to = "rate", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(regime = factor(regime, levels = c("No taxes (1958)", "Corporate tax of 25 percent (1963)")),
         rate = factor(rate, levels = c("Cost of equity", "WACC", "Cost of debt")))
ggplot(mm, aes(L, value, colour = rate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~regime) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal[c("orange", "blue", "aqua")])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.32)) +
  labs(x = "Debt as a share of firm value (D/V)", y = "Required return", colour = NULL,
       title = "Leverage and the cost of capital",
       caption = "Illustrative: return on assets 10 percent, pre-tax cost of debt 5 percent (shown after tax in the right panel), permanent debt.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The MM propositions are not empirical predictions in the usual sense. Their
importance lies in what they imply about where to look. If financing matters, it must
be because one of the assumptions fails. Table \@ref(tab:tab-fin-mm-assumptions)
maps the main research programs in corporate finance onto the assumptions they
relax, which is why MM is often described as the foundation of the field rather than a
description of it [@myers2001].

```{r tab-fin-mm-assumptions}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`MM assumption`, ~`What happens when it fails`, ~`Resulting theory`, ~`Key reference`,
  "No corporate taxes", "Interest deductibility makes debt valuable", "Tax shield, static trade-off", "Modigliani & Miller (1963)",
  "No costs of financial distress", "Expected bankruptcy and distress costs offset tax benefits", "[Trade-off theory](#trade-off-pecking-order)", "Kraus & Litzenberger (1973)",
  "Symmetric information", "Equity issues signal overvaluation, internal funds are preferred", "[Pecking order theory](#trade-off-pecking-order)", "Myers & Majluf (1984)",
  "No agency conflicts", "Debt and payouts discipline managers with surplus cash", "[Free cash flow theory](#free-cash-flow)", "Jensen (1986)",
  "Investment policy fixed", "Debt overhang causes underinvestment in good projects", "Debt overhang", "Myers (1977)",
  "Prices equal fundamental value", "Managers issue equity when it is overpriced", "Market timing", "Baker & Wurgler (2002)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The Modigliani-Miller assumptions as a map of corporate finance.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Irrelevance as a benchmark or as a claim?** Critics sometimes dismiss MM as
unrealistic. Its defenders reply that unrealistic assumptions are the point: the
theorems isolate the conditions under which financing could matter, and every later
theory in this chapter is a precise answer to the question "which friction?" The
remaining debate is quantitative: how large are the tax benefits of debt after
personal taxes, and how large are expected distress costs? Those magnitudes have
proved hard to pin down, as the next section shows.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Taxes and the Apple bond issue of 2013.** In April 2013 Apple sold 17 billion
dollars of bonds, at the time one of the largest corporate bond offerings on record,
even though it held well over 100 billion dollars in cash and securities. A large
share of that cash was held by foreign subsidiaries, and bringing it home would
have triggered US taxes under the rules then in force. Borrowing at low interest
rates to fund dividends and share repurchases let Apple return cash to shareholders
without paying the repatriation tax, and the interest was tax deductible. The case
illustrates the MM logic in reverse: financing decisions create value precisely when
a friction, here the tax code, breaks the irrelevance conditions.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Exogenous increases in corporate tax rates lead firms to increase leverage,
  and the effect is larger for firms with fewer non-debt tax shields.
- *H2.* The equity beta of a firm rises with leverage as predicted by Proposition II
  after controlling for asset beta.

**Designs.** Natural experiments from tax reforms, staggered state tax changes,
regression of equity betas on leverage, event studies of pure recapitalisations.

**Data.** Compustat fundamentals, CRSP returns, tax rate databases, bond issuance
data (Mergent FISD).
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Reading MM as "capital structure does not matter".** The theorems say that capital
structure is irrelevant *only* under perfect markets, which makes them a checklist of
reasons why it does matter. A second misuse is to apply Proposition II's logic
backward: a lower WACC from adding debt is not evidence of value creation unless
the cost of equity has been adjusted for the higher financial risk.
:::

## Trade-off and Pecking Order Theories {#trade-off-pecking-order}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** The **static trade-off theory** holds that firms choose a target
leverage that balances the tax benefits of debt against the expected costs of
financial distress. The **pecking order theory** holds that, because of information
asymmetry, firms prefer internal funds to debt and debt to equity, so leverage is the
cumulative result of past financing needs rather than a target.

**Origins.** Finance. @kraus1973 formalised the trade-off. @myers1984a and
@myers1984 developed the pecking order. @shyamsunder1999 and @frank2003 set up the
classic empirical contest.

**Level of analysis.** Firm.

**Key constructs.** Target leverage, interest tax shield, costs of financial
distress, debt overhang, financing deficit, financial slack, adverse selection cost
of equity, market timing.

**Boundary conditions.** Trade-off logic requires meaningful tax benefits and
distress costs. Pecking order logic requires managers to know more than investors
and to act in the interest of existing shareholders.

**Related theories.** [Modigliani-Miller](#modigliani-miller),
[Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry) (Section \@ref(information-asymmetry)), [Signaling theory](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)),
[Free cash flow theory](#free-cash-flow).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Once @modigliani1963 showed that debt creates a tax shield, the obvious puzzle was why
firms are not financed almost entirely with debt. @kraus1973 provided the standard
answer in a state-preference model: debt creates tax savings in good states but
deadweight bankruptcy costs in bad ones, so there is an interior optimum. Later work
added the indirect costs of distress, such as lost customers and suppliers, and
@myers1977 identified **debt overhang**: a heavily indebted firm may forgo valuable
projects because much of their payoff would go to creditors.

In his 1984 presidential address to the American Finance Association, published as
"The Capital Structure Puzzle", @myers1984a argued that the trade-off theory fits the
data poorly. Many highly profitable firms, which have the most taxable income to
shield, borrow the least. He proposed instead a **pecking order** grounded in the
asymmetric information model of @myers1984. If managers know more than investors
about the value of the firm, they will be most willing to issue equity when it is
overvalued. Investors understand this and treat an equity issue as bad news, so
issuing equity is expensive for good firms. Internal funds avoid the problem
entirely, and safe debt nearly does. The result is a financing hierarchy.

### Core logic and propositions

The trade-off theory can be written as

$$V_L = V_U + \text{PV}(\text{interest tax shields}) - \text{PV}(\text{costs of financial distress}),$$

with the optimal debt level where the marginal tax benefit equals the marginal
expected distress cost. The pecking order is usually tested with the financing
deficit, the cash a firm must raise externally:

$$\text{DEF}_t = \text{DIV}_t + X_t + \Delta W_t + R_t - C_t, \qquad
\Delta D_{it} = a + b_{\text{PO}} \, \text{DEF}_{it} + e_{it},$$

where DIV is dividends, $X$ capital expenditure, $\Delta W$ the increase in working
capital, $R$ the current portion of long-term debt, and $C$ operating cash flow after
interest and taxes. Under a strict pecking order, debt fills the deficit one for one,
so $a = 0$ and $b_{\text{PO}} = 1$ [@shyamsunder1999].

- **P1 (Trade-off: target).** Firms have target leverage ratios and adjust toward them.
- **P2 (Trade-off: cross-section).** Leverage rises with tax benefits and tangible
  assets and falls with distress costs, earnings volatility, and growth options.
- **P3 (Pecking order: hierarchy).** Firms use internal funds first, then debt, and
  issue equity only as a last resort.
- **P4 (Pecking order: profitability).** More profitable firms use less debt because
  they need less external finance.
- **P5 (Pecking order: announcement effects).** Announcements of equity issues are
  followed by negative abnormal returns, and the effect is larger when information
  asymmetry is greater.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-tradeoff) shows the trade-off. The MM tax line rises without
limit. Distress costs are negligible at low leverage and rise steeply as default
becomes likely, so firm value peaks at an interior debt level.

```{r fig-fin-tradeoff, fig.cap = "Illustrative static trade-off theory. The interest tax shield raises firm value linearly with debt, while the present value of financial distress costs rises with leverage. Firm value peaks at an interior optimum, marked by the dashed line.", fig.height = 4}
tradeoff <- tibble::tibble(d = seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.005)) |>
  mutate(`All-equity value (MM 1958)` = 100,
         `With tax shield only (MM 1963)` = 100 + 25 * d,
         `Trade-off: tax shield minus distress costs` = 100 + 25 * d - 52 * d^3) |>
  pivot_longer(-d, names_to = "line", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(line = factor(line, levels = c("With tax shield only (MM 1963)",
                                        "Trade-off: tax shield minus distress costs",
                                        "All-equity value (MM 1958)")))
d_star <- sqrt(25 / (3 * 52))
v_star <- 100 + 25 * d_star - 52 * d_star^3
ggplot(tradeoff, aes(d, value, colour = line)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = d_star, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("point", x = d_star, y = v_star, size = 3, colour = pal[["blue"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = d_star + 0.015, y = v_star + 2.2, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = sprintf("Optimal debt = %.0f percent of unlevered value", 100 * d_star)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal[c("orange", "blue", "aqua")])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Debt as a share of unlevered firm value", y = "Firm value (unlevered = 100)", colour = NULL,
       title = "The static trade-off between tax benefits and distress costs",
       caption = "Illustrative: tax shield = 0.25 x D, PV of distress costs = 52 x d^3, where d = D / V_U.")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-pecking) summarises the pecking order mechanism. The cost of
each source of funds rises with its sensitivity to managers' private information.

```{r fig-fin-pecking, fig.cap = "Mechanism of the pecking order theory. Because managers know more than investors, securities whose value depends more on that private information carry a larger adverse selection discount. Firms therefore finance with internal funds first, then debt, and equity last. Financial slack relaxes the constraint."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  A [label = "Information asymmetry\\n(managers know more\\nabout firm value)", %s]
  S [label = "Adverse selection\\ndiscount on\\nrisky securities", %s]
  F1 [label = "1. Internal funds\\n(retained earnings)", %s]
  F2 [label = "2. Debt\\n(safe, then risky)", %s]
  F3 [label = "3. External equity\\n(last resort)", %s]
  L [label = "Observed leverage\\n= cumulative\\nfinancing deficits", %s]
  K [label = "Financial slack\\n(cash, unused\\ndebt capacity)", %s]
  A -> S
  S -> F1 [label = " none"]
  S -> F2 [label = " small"]
  S -> F3 [label = " large"]
  F1 -> F2 -> F3 [style = dotted]
  F2 -> L
  K -> S [style = dashed, arrowhead = tee]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

The two theories make sharply different predictions, summarised in Table
\@ref(tab:tab-fin-tradeoff-pecking). The empirical contest has run for four decades
without a clear winner.

```{r tab-fin-tradeoff-pecking}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Issue, ~`Static trade-off`, ~`Pecking order`, ~`What the evidence suggests`,
  "Target leverage", "Yes, firms adjust toward it", "No well-defined target", "Mixed: adjustment is slow, leverage is highly persistent",
  "Profitability and leverage", "Positive (more taxable income to shield)", "Negative (less need for external funds)", "Negative, favouring the pecking order",
  "Response to financing deficit", "Partial, depends on distance from target", "Debt fills the deficit one for one", "Strong for large mature firms, weak for small growth firms",
  "Equity issuance", "When leverage is above target", "Rare, a last resort", "Small growth firms issue equity often",
  "Market reaction to equity issues", "Neutral", "Negative", "Negative on average",
  "Role of stock prices", "None", "None directly", "Firms issue equity after price run-ups (market timing)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Contrasting predictions of the static trade-off and pecking order theories.")
```

@shyamsunder1999 found that for a sample of large, mature US firms, net debt issues
tracked the financing deficit closely, which favoured the pecking order, and that
standard target-adjustment tests had little power to distinguish the two theories.
@frank2003 extended the test to a much broader sample of US firms and found that net
equity issues tracked the deficit more closely than net debt issues. Small,
high-growth firms, where information asymmetry and hence the pecking order should be
strongest, issued the most equity. The pecking order fit best for large firms.

Two further findings complicate both theories. @lemmon2008 showed that leverage is
remarkably persistent, with most of its variation explained by a stable firm effect
that standard determinants do not capture. @baker2002 argued that firms issue
equity when their market values are high relative to book and past market values, and
that these **market timing** decisions have long-lasting effects on capital structure.
In survey evidence, CFOs stressed financial flexibility and credit ratings, and few
described their leverage target as strict [@graham2001].

::: {.debate}
**Is there a capital structure theory at all?** @myers2001 concluded that there is no
universal theory of the debt-equity choice, only conditional theories that work in
different settings: trade-off logic for differences across industries, pecking order
logic for the profitability effect and issue announcements, market timing for bursts
of issuance in hot markets. A further critique is econometric: leverage ratios
are mechanically mean-reverting, so finding "adjustment toward a target" does not by
itself confirm the trade-off theory [@shyamsunder1999].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Leverage decisions in practice.** Firms in the same economy choose strikingly
different capital structures, and the differences line up with trade-off logic.
Regulated utilities and real estate investment trusts, whose cash flows are stable and
whose assets are tangible and redeployable, routinely carry high leverage. Technology
and biotechnology firms, whose value lies in growth options and intangible assets that
would lose much of their value in distress, typically carry little net debt, and many
hold large cash balances. Within those broad patterns, pecking order and timing
behaviour are easy to observe. Announcements of seasoned equity offerings are, on
average, followed by negative stock price reactions, consistent with @myers1984.
Conversely, firms whose shares have run up issue equity opportunistically. In 2021,
after the run-up in their share prices described in the
[Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance) section, GameStop and AMC Entertainment both
sold new shares through at-the-market offerings, using a high stock price to raise
capital and reduce debt, which is market timing in the sense of @baker2002.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The negative relation between profitability and leverage is stronger for
  firms with greater information asymmetry (fewer analysts, more intangible assets).
- *H2.* Firms issue more equity when their market-to-book ratio is high relative to
  its historical average, controlling for investment opportunities.

**Measures.** Book and market leverage, financing deficit, market-to-book ratio,
asset tangibility, marginal tax rates, distance to default, analyst forecast
dispersion as a proxy for information asymmetry.

**Designs.** Partial adjustment models of leverage, financing deficit regressions,
event studies of security issues, natural experiments from tax and bankruptcy law
changes, surveys of CFOs.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating every cross-sectional correlation as a test of one theory.** Profitability,
size, tangibility, and growth opportunities are related to leverage under several
theories at once, often with the same sign. A negative profitability coefficient is
consistent with the pecking order but also with mean reversion in leverage and with
agency explanations. Specify which prediction is *unique* to the theory you are
testing, and use settings where the theories diverge.
:::

## Free Cash Flow Theory {#free-cash-flow}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When a firm generates more cash than it can invest in positive net
present value projects, self-interested managers tend to waste the surplus on
low-return growth rather than return it to shareholders. Debt, payouts, and the market
for corporate control reduce these agency costs.

**Origins.** Finance and organisational economics. @jensen1986, building on the
agency framework of @jensen1976.

**Level of analysis.** Firm and top management.

**Key constructs.** Free cash flow, empire building, agency costs of equity, debt as
a bonding device, payout policy, leveraged buyout, market for corporate control.

**Boundary conditions.** Firms have substantial cash flows and limited growth
opportunities, and managerial incentives are imperfectly aligned with shareholders'.
The theory has least force for young, high-growth firms with more good projects than
cash.

**Related theories.** [Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)),
[Stewardship theory](#stewardship-theory) (Section \@ref(stewardship-theory)),
[Upper echelons theory](#upper-echelons-theory) (Section \@ref(upper-echelons-theory)),
[Modigliani-Miller](#modigliani-miller).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Jensen's 1986 paper applied the agency framework of @jensen1976 to a specific
question: what happens to cash a firm does not need? He defined **free cash flow** as
cash flow in excess of that required to fund all projects with positive net present
value at the relevant cost of capital. Managers, he argued, want firms to grow beyond
their optimal size because size brings power, status, and pay, and free cash flow
fuels that growth. Jensen used the theory to explain the takeovers and leveraged
buyouts of the 1980s, and he pointed to
the oil industry, where high prices in the late 1970s generated large cash flows that
many companies reinvested in exploration and diversification even as the returns to
such investment declined [@jensen1986].

### Core logic and propositions

- **P1 (Overinvestment).** Firms with high free cash flow and poor investment
  opportunities overinvest, for instance in diversifying acquisitions, and these
  investments earn low returns.
- **P2 (Debt as bonding).** Debt commits managers to pay out future cash flows,
  reducing the cash available for waste. Unlike a promise to pay dividends, debt
  payments are enforceable through bankruptcy.
- **P3 (Payouts).** Increases in dividends and repurchases by firms with free cash flow
  problems are good news for shareholders. Cuts are bad news.
- **P4 (Control market).** Takeovers and leveraged buyouts create value
  disproportionately in firms with large free cash flow and few growth opportunities.

### Mechanism

```{r fig-fin-fcf, fig.cap = "Mechanism of free cash flow theory. Surplus cash combined with weak growth opportunities and managerial empire-building incentives leads to overinvestment and value destruction. Debt, payouts, takeovers, and incentive pay reduce the cash available for waste."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  C [label = "Free cash flow\\n(cash beyond all\\npositive-NPV projects)", %s]
  G [label = "Limited growth\\nopportunities", %s]
  M [label = "Managerial preference\\nfor size, perks, control", %s]
  O [label = "Overinvestment and\\nvalue-destroying\\nacquisitions", %s]
  V [label = "Lower firm value\\n(agency costs)", %s]
  D [label = "Debt service", %s]
  P [label = "Dividends and\\nbuybacks", %s]
  T [label = "Takeover threat\\nand LBOs", %s]
  C -> O
  G -> O
  M -> O
  O -> V
  D -> C [style = dashed, arrowhead = tee]
  P -> C [style = dashed, arrowhead = tee]
  T -> M [style = dashed, arrowhead = tee]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome,
   node_moderator, node_moderator, node_moderator))
```

The governance devices in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-fcf) differ in strength and cost,
as Table \@ref(tab:tab-fin-fcf-devices) summarises. The trade-off between them echoes
the general logic of [Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)): every disciplinary device is
itself costly, and the efficient mix depends on how severe the agency problem is.

```{r tab-fin-fcf-devices}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Device, ~`How it reduces free cash flow problems`, ~`Commitment strength`, ~`Main cost or risk`,
  "Regular dividends", "Pays out cash and creates an expectation of continuation", "Moderate (cuts are penalised but legal)", "Personal taxes, inflexibility in downturns",
  "Share repurchases", "Returns cash flexibly", "Weak (no ongoing commitment)", "Can be timed opportunistically or used to manage earnings per share",
  "Debt", "Contractually pre-commits future cash flows", "Strong (default triggers bankruptcy)", "Financial distress, debt overhang",
  "Leveraged buyout", "Combines high debt, concentrated ownership, and equity incentives", "Very strong", "Fragility if cash flows fall, high transaction costs",
  "Hostile takeover threat", "Replaces managers who waste cash", "Depends on legal defences", "Disruption, short-termism concerns",
  "Equity-based pay", "Aligns managers with shareholder value", "Moderate", "Risk-taking, manipulation of timing"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Devices that discipline the use of free cash flow.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

@kaplan1989 studied management buyouts of public companies in the 1980s and found
that operating income rose, capital expenditure fell, and net cash flow increased in
the years after the buyout, consistent with the view that high leverage and
concentrated ownership improved the use of cash. @harford1999 found that cash-rich
firms were more likely to attempt acquisitions and that those acquisitions were
followed by abnormal declines in operating performance, which is the overinvestment
the theory predicts. Managerial overconfidence [@malmendier2005] and hubris
[@roll1986] predict the same overinvestment without conscious self-interest, a
distinction that matters for remedies.

Payout policy is the natural testing ground. @lintner1956 found that managers set
dividends with a long-run target payout ratio in mind and adjust gradually,
reluctant to raise dividends they might later have to cut. Half a century later,
@brav2005 found that this reluctance remained strong and that repurchases had become
the preferred flexible tool for distributing cash. Dividends can also
signal private information about future cash flows [@bhattacharya1979], and the
signaling and free cash flow accounts are not mutually exclusive.

::: {.debate}
**Agency problem or precaution?** Free cash flow theory reads large cash holdings as
a symptom of agency problems. An alternative view is precautionary: firms with
volatile cash flows, high R&D, and limited access to debt markets hold cash to avoid
having to pass up good projects in bad times, a motive rooted in the pecking order.
A second debate concerns buybacks. Critics argue that repurchases divert cash from
investment and let managers time sales of their own shares. Defenders reply that
returning cash that cannot be profitably invested is exactly what Jensen recommended.
Adjudicating requires knowing whether the firm forwent positive NPV projects, which
is hard to observe.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**The RJR Nabisco buyout.** The largest leveraged buyout of the 1980s, the 1989
acquisition of RJR Nabisco by Kohlberg Kravis Roberts, was widely interpreted through
Jensen's lens. The company's tobacco business generated large, stable cash flows with
limited reinvestment needs, which made it a classic free cash flow firm. The buyout
replaced public equity with heavy debt, forcing the company to devote its cash flow to
interest and principal and to sell assets. The episode, which followed a contested
bidding process, became a public symbol both of the disciplinary logic of debt and of
the risks of paying too much in a competitive auction.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Dividend and buyback policy at mature technology firms.** As large technology
companies matured, their free cash flow came to exceed what they could invest
internally. Apple announced in 2012 that it would begin paying a dividend and
repurchasing shares, and it has since returned very large amounts of cash through
buybacks and dividends. Microsoft began paying dividends in 2003 and paid a large
special dividend in 2004. Such policies combine free cash flow logic (return cash
that cannot be invested at high returns), [Signaling](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)) (a regular
dividend conveys confidence in future cash flows), and flexibility (buybacks can be
scaled without the penalty attached to a dividend cut). The practical checklist:
estimate free cash flow after all positive NPV investment, commit a sustainable part
through regular dividends, and use repurchases for the residual.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The announcement return to a diversifying acquisition is more negative when
  the acquirer has high free cash flow and low Tobin's q.
- *H2.* Firms that increase leverage through recapitalisations subsequently reduce
  capital expenditure and improve operating margins, more so when prior free cash flow
  was high.

**Measures.** Free cash flow scaled by assets, Tobin's q as a proxy for growth
opportunities, excess cash relative to a predicted benchmark, governance indices,
payout ratios, acquisition announcements.

**Designs.** Event studies, panel regressions with firm fixed effects, natural
experiments from changes in takeover law (such as state anti-takeover statutes) or
dividend taxation, comparisons of buyout firms with matched controls.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating cash with waste.** Not all large cash balances signal an agency problem.
Before concluding that cash is "free", estimate the firm's investment opportunities,
its access to external finance, and the volatility of its cash flows. The theory
predicts waste only when cash exceeds what positive NPV projects and prudent
precaution require.
:::

## Limits to Arbitrage {#limits-to-arbitrage}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Correcting mispricing requires capital and bears risk. Because real
arbitrage is risky, capital constrained, and often delegated to professionals who
answer to impatient investors, mispricing can persist and even widen before it
corrects.

**Origins.** Finance. @delong1990 on noise trader risk and @shleifer1997 on
performance-based arbitrage, synthesised in @shleifer2000.

**Level of analysis.** Arbitrageur and market.

**Key constructs.** Fundamental risk, noise trader risk, implementation costs,
short-sale constraints, performance-based arbitrage, forced liquidation, synchronisation
risk.

**Boundary conditions.** Mispricing must be uncertain in duration or magnitude,
arbitrage capital must be limited, and close substitutes for the mispriced asset must
be imperfect or costly to trade.

**Related theories.** [Efficient market hypothesis](#efficient-market-hypothesis),
[Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance), [Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)),
[Collective action](#collective-action) (Section \@ref(collective-action)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The classical defence of efficiency, associated with Milton Friedman and with
@fama1970, holds that irrational traders cannot affect prices for long, because
arbitrageurs trade against them and irrational traders lose money and disappear.
@delong1990 challenged both halves of the argument. If noise traders' beliefs are
unpredictable, an arbitrageur betting against today's mispricing risks that it gets
worse tomorrow. With short horizons, this **noise trader risk** limits arbitrage, so
prices can diverge from fundamentals even with no fundamental risk at all. Noise traders may even
earn higher average returns than rational investors because they bear more of the
risk they themselves create.

@shleifer1997 added an organisational dimension. Arbitrage is conducted by
specialised professionals managing other people's money, and investors judge them by
recent returns. When a mispricing widens, the arbitrageur shows losses just as the
opportunity becomes most attractive, investors withdraw capital, and the arbitrageur
may be forced to liquidate at the worst moment. This is
**performance-based arbitrage**, and it makes arbitrage least effective when it is
most needed.

### Core logic and propositions

In the overlapping generations model of @delong1990, a safe asset and an unsafe asset
pay the same dividend, so the unsafe asset's fundamental value is 1. A fraction $\mu$
of investors are noise traders whose misperception of the expected return is
$\rho_t$, normally distributed with mean $\rho^{*}$ and variance $\sigma_\rho^2$.
Rational investors have risk aversion $\gamma$, and $r$ is the riskless rate. The
equilibrium price is

$$p_t = 1 + \frac{\mu\left(\rho_t - \rho^{*}\right)}{1+r} + \frac{\mu \rho^{*}}{r} -
\frac{2\gamma \mu^2 \sigma_\rho^2}{r(1+r)^2}.$$

The second term moves the price with current noise trader sentiment, the third
captures their average optimism or pessimism, and the last is a discount for the
risk that noise traders' beliefs will change. Although the asset's fundamental value
is certain, its price is volatile, and unless noise traders are optimistic enough on
average it trades below fundamental value, because rational investors must be paid
to bear the risk that noise traders create.

- **P1 (Noise trader risk).** When arbitrageurs have finite horizons, mispricing
  driven by investor sentiment can persist even without fundamental risk.
- **P2 (Performance-based arbitrage).** When arbitrage capital is delegated and
  investors withdraw after losses, arbitrageurs are least able to trade when
  mispricing is greatest.
- **P3 (Where anomalies live).** Mispricing is larger and more persistent in assets
  that are costly to short, volatile, and lacking close substitutes.
- **P4 (Crowding and liquidation).** When many arbitrageurs hold similar positions,
  forced selling by some can worsen mispricing for all.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-arb) simulates a stylised episode. An arbitrageur identifies
an 8 percent mispricing between two securities with identical cash flows and takes a
leveraged position. Noise trader sentiment widens the gap to almost 30 percent before it
eventually closes. A leveraged fund whose investors withdraw after losses is forced to
liquidate near the trough and never recovers, while patient capital holding exactly the
same position eventually profits.

```{r fig-fin-arb, fig.cap = "Illustrative performance-based arbitrage. Top: the mispricing between two claims on identical cash flows widens before it converges. Bottom: a leveraged arbitrage fund facing investor withdrawals is forced to liquidate near the worst point, while patient capital with the same position ends with a gain.", fig.height = 5.2}
set.seed(1997)
t_w <- 0:100
shape <- ifelse(t_w <= 40, -8 - 17 * (t_w / 40)^1.5, -25 * pmax(0, 1 - (t_w - 40) / 60)^1.5)
mis <- shape + c(0, cumsum(rnorm(100, 0, 0.3))) * ifelse(t_w > 90, (100 - t_w) / 10, 1)
mis[1] <- -8
patient <- 100 + 3 * (mis - mis[1])
forced <- patient
hit <- which(patient < 65)[1]
if (!is.na(hit)) forced[hit:length(forced)] <- patient[hit]
arb <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(week = t_w, value = mis, series = "Mispricing (percent)", panel = "Mispricing between twin securities (percent)"),
  tibble::tibble(week = t_w, value = patient, series = "Patient capital, same position", panel = "Arbitrage capital (index, start = 100)"),
  tibble::tibble(week = t_w, value = forced, series = "Leveraged fund forced to liquidate", panel = "Arbitrage capital (index, start = 100)")
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Mispricing between twin securities (percent)", "Arbitrage capital (index, start = 100)")),
         series = factor(series, levels = c("Mispricing (percent)", "Patient capital, same position",
                                            "Leveraged fund forced to liquidate")))
ggplot(arb, aes(week, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_hline(data = data.frame(panel = factor(c("Mispricing between twin securities (percent)", "Arbitrage capital (index, start = 100)"),
                                              levels = levels(arb$panel)), y = c(0, 100)),
             aes(yintercept = y), colour = ink[["muted"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal[c("blue", "aqua", "orange")])) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Weeks since the arbitrage position was opened", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "Right on fundamentals, wrong on timing",
       caption = "Illustrative simulation: position leverage 3x, forced liquidation when capital falls below 65 percent of its starting value.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The cleanest evidence comes from securities whose relative value is fixed by contract.
Table \@ref(tab:tab-fin-arb-cases) summarises four well-documented episodes.

```{r tab-fin-arb-cases}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Episode, ~`What should have held`, ~`What happened`, ~`Limit to arbitrage`,
  "Royal Dutch and Shell (Froot & Dabora 1999)", "Twin shares with a fixed split of cash flows should trade at a constant price ratio", "The ratio deviated substantially from parity for years", "Noise trader risk with no fixed convergence date",
  "Palm and 3Com, 2000 (Lamont & Thaler 2003)", "3Com, which still owned most of Palm, should be worth at least its Palm stake", "The market implied a negative value for 3Com's other businesses", "Short-sale constraints on Palm shares",
  "Long-Term Capital Management, 1998", "Convergence trades should profit as spreads narrow", "Spreads widened sharply after the Russian default and the fund lost most of its capital", "Leverage, crowding, and forced liquidation",
