  "GameStop, January 2021 (SEC 2021)", "Prices should reflect expected cash flows", "The price rose roughly twentyfold in weeks and remained volatile", "Short-selling risk, margin calls, and coordinated noise trading"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Episodes illustrating the limits to arbitrage.")
```

The Royal Dutch and Shell case is particularly instructive. Under their 1907
alliance, cash flows were split 60 to 40, so Royal Dutch should have been worth 1.5
times Shell. @froot1999 showed that the ratio deviated from parity by large amounts
for long periods. An arbitrageur betting on convergence faced no fundamental risk,
only the risk that the deviation would widen, with no date by which it had to close.

::: {.debate}
**Does limited arbitrage rescue or bury the EMH?** Defenders of efficiency note that
in each famous case the mispricing was eventually corrected and that it is hard to
profit from these episodes after transaction costs. Behavioural economists reply that
this is exactly the point: "no free lunch" does not imply "prices are right"
[@barberis2003]. If even riskless relative mispricing can persist, mispricing of
whole markets, with no close substitute and no convergence date, can persist far
longer. Still, [limits to arbitrage](#limits-to-arbitrage) explain why mispricing *can* persist, not which
direction it takes. That requires a theory of investor beliefs.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Long-Term Capital Management, 1998.** LTCM was founded in 1994 by John Meriwether,
and its partners included Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the 1997 Nobel
Memorial Prize for their work on option pricing. The fund specialised in convergence
and relative-value trades, such as buying less liquid bonds and selling more liquid
but otherwise similar bonds, betting that small price gaps would close. Because each
gap was small, the strategy required very high leverage. After Russia defaulted on
its domestic debt in August 1998, investors worldwide fled to the safest and most
liquid securities. The spreads LTCM had bet would narrow widened instead, and because
many other traders held similar positions, attempts to reduce risk pushed prices
further against the fund. By September its capital had collapsed, and the Federal
Reserve Bank of New York convened a group of major banks and securities firms that
recapitalised the fund with about 3.6 billion dollars to avoid a disorderly
liquidation [@lowenstein2000; @pwg1999]. The episode is the textbook illustration of
@shleifer1997, published a year earlier: arbitrage can fail when capital is
leveraged, crowded, and impatient. Risk managers should stress-test for widening
spreads and crowded positions.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Anomaly returns are larger among stocks with higher short-selling costs
  (lower institutional ownership, higher lending fees).
- *H2.* Hedge fund outflows following poor performance predict subsequent widening of
  mispricing in the stocks those funds hold.

**Measures.** Mispricing in contractually linked securities, idiosyncratic volatility
as arbitrage risk, short interest and loan fees, fund flows, funding liquidity spreads.

**Designs.** Cross-sectional tests that interact anomaly signals with limits to
arbitrage proxies, natural experiments from short-sale bans or changes in lending
supply, case studies of contractually linked securities.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Using limits to arbitrage as a universal escape hatch.** Almost any failure of a
mispricing to correct can be attributed, after the fact, to some limit to arbitrage.
To make the theory testable, specify *in advance* which limit (short-sale costs,
idiosyncratic risk, capital constraints) should matter, measure it, and predict that
mispricing will be greater where that limit is tighter.
:::

## Behavioral Finance {#behavioral-finance}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Investor psychology produces systematic errors in beliefs and
preferences, and because arbitrage is limited, these errors affect prices, trading,
and corporate decisions.

**Origins.** Finance, economics, and psychology. Early contributions include
@shefrin1985 and @delong1990. @barberis2003 is the standard survey. Robert Shiller
received the Nobel Memorial Prize in 2013 and Richard Thaler in 2017.

**Level of analysis.** Individual investor, manager, and market.

**Key constructs.** Overconfidence, disposition effect, extrapolation, limited
attention, [loss aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)), mental accounting, investor sentiment, market timing.

**Boundary conditions.** Biases must be systematic (shared across many investors) to
affect prices, and arbitrage must be costly. Effects are strongest for assets that are
hard to value and hard to arbitrage.

**Related theories.** [Limits to arbitrage](#limits-to-arbitrage),
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory-model) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-model)), [Disposition effect](#disposition-effect) (Section \@ref(disposition-effect)),
[Heuristics and biases](#heuristics-biases) (Section \@ref(heuristics-biases)), [Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)),
[Conformity](#conformity) (Section \@ref(conformity)), [Social transmission](#social-transmission) (Section \@ref(social-transmission)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Behavioural finance grew from the confluence of two ideas. From psychology came
evidence that people deviate systematically from expected utility and Bayesian
updating, especially the work of Kahneman and Tversky on judgment under uncertainty and
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory-model) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-model)) [@kahneman1979]. From finance came the
realisation, formalised by @delong1990 and @shleifer1997, that rational arbitrage need
not eliminate the price effects of irrational traders. @barberis2003 describe the
field as resting on these two building blocks: limits to arbitrage, which explain
why mispricing can survive, and psychology, which explains what form it takes.

### Core logic and propositions

- **P1 (Overconfidence and trading).** Investors who overestimate the precision of
  their information trade too much and earn lower net returns.
- **P2 (Disposition effect).** Investors realise gains more readily than losses, a
  pattern consistent with [prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)) and mental accounting.
- **P3 (Sentiment).** Waves of investor optimism and pessimism move the prices of
  hard-to-value, hard-to-arbitrage stocks more than others, and high sentiment
  predicts low subsequent returns for those stocks.
- **P4 (Managerial response).** Managers respond to mispricing by issuing equity when
  it is overvalued and buying back shares when it is undervalued, and their own
  biases shape investment.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-behav) shows how the building blocks combine. Psychological
biases generate correlated demand. Limits to arbitrage allow that demand to move
prices. Mispricing then feeds back into corporate decisions through equity issuance,
repurchases, and investment.

```{r fig-fin-behav, fig.cap = "Mechanism of behavioural finance. Systematic biases create correlated noise trading. When arbitrage is limited, prices deviate from fundamentals, which affects returns and induces managers to time security issues and repurchases."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  B [label = "Investor biases\\n(overconfidence,\\nextrapolation, disposition)", %s]
  S [label = "Investor sentiment\\nand social contagion", %s]
  N [label = "Correlated\\nnoise trading", %s]
  M [label = "Mispricing", %s]
  R [label = "Predictable returns\\n(reversals, drift)", %s]
  C [label = "Corporate response\\n(issuance, buybacks,\\ninvestment)", %s]
  L [label = "Limits to arbitrage\\n(short costs, risk,\\ncapital)", %s]
  B -> N
  S -> N
  N -> M
  M -> R
  M -> C
  L -> M [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

**Overconfidence.** Using records from a large discount brokerage, @barber2000 found
that the households that traded most earned substantially lower net returns than the
market, largely because of trading costs. @barber2001 then used gender as a proxy for
overconfidence, motivated by evidence that men are more overconfident than women in
domains such as finance. Men traded about 45 percent more than women, and trading
reduced men's net returns by more than it reduced women's.

**Disposition effect.** @shefrin1985 argued that investors are predisposed to sell
winners too early and ride losers too long. @odean1998 confirmed the pattern in
brokerage data: investors realised a higher proportion of their gains than of their
losses, and the winners they sold went on to outperform the losers they kept. See
the [Disposition effect](#disposition-effect) (Section \@ref(disposition-effect)) for a full treatment.

**Investor sentiment.** @baker2006 built a composite sentiment index from proxies
such as the closed-end fund discount, share turnover, the number and first-day returns
of IPOs, the equity share of new issues, and the dividend premium. When sentiment was
high, subsequent returns were relatively low for small, young, highly volatile,
unprofitable, non-dividend-paying, extreme growth, and distressed stocks, and when
sentiment was low the pattern reversed. These are exactly the stocks that are hardest
to value and hardest to arbitrage, as P3 predicts. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-fin-sentiment)
sketches the pattern.

```{r fig-fin-sentiment, fig.cap = "Stylised pattern of sentiment and subsequent returns. Hard-to-value stocks earn low returns after periods of high sentiment and high returns after periods of low sentiment, while easy-to-value stocks are little affected. Not empirical data.", fig.height = 3.8}
sent <- tibble::tibble(
  stocks = factor(rep(c("Easy to value and arbitrage\n(large, old, profitable, dividend payers)",
                        "Hard to value and arbitrage\n(small, young, volatile, unprofitable)"), each = 2),
                  levels = c("Easy to value and arbitrage\n(large, old, profitable, dividend payers)",
                             "Hard to value and arbitrage\n(small, young, volatile, unprofitable)")),
  regime = factor(rep(c("After high sentiment", "After low sentiment"), 2),
                  levels = c("After high sentiment", "After low sentiment")),
  ret = c(0.08, 0.10, -0.01, 0.17)
)
ggplot(sent, aes(stocks, ret, fill = regime)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(ret, 1)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = ifelse(sent$ret >= 0, -0.4, 1.3), size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("orange", "blue")])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(-0.04, 0.2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Subsequent annual return", fill = NULL,
       title = "Sentiment matters most where arbitrage is hardest",
       caption = "Stylised pattern consistent with Baker and Wurgler (2006). Values are illustrative, not estimates.")
```

**Corporate decisions.** Rational managers can exploit mispricing by timing equity
issues [@baker2002], and managers have biases too: overconfident CEOs overinvest
[@malmendier2005] and acquirers may overpay because of hubris [@roll1986]. Table
\@ref(tab:tab-fin-biases) organises the main findings.

```{r tab-fin-biases}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Bias, ~`Psychological root`, ~`Market or firm consequence`, ~`Key evidence`, ~`Practical implication`,
  "Overconfidence", "Miscalibrated precision of private information", "Excessive trading, lower net returns", "Barber & Odean (2000, 2001)", "Default to low-turnover strategies, cost disclosure",
  "Disposition effect", "Prospect theory, mental accounting, regret", "Selling winners and holding losers, drift after news", "Shefrin & Statman (1985), Odean (1998)", "Rule-based selling, tax-loss harvesting",
  "Extrapolation", "Representativeness, recency", "Overpricing of glamour stocks, reversals", "Barberis & Thaler (2003)", "Skepticism toward trend-based forecasts",
  "Limited attention", "Finite cognitive resources", "Underreaction to news, earnings drift", "Bernard & Thomas (1989)", "Timing and salience of disclosures",
  "Sentiment", "Correlated mood and beliefs", "Mispricing of hard-to-value stocks", "Baker & Wurgler (2006)", "Equity issuance when sentiment is high",
  "Managerial overconfidence", "Better-than-average beliefs", "Overinvestment and costly acquisitions", "Malmendier & Tate (2005), Roll (1986)", "Independent boards, investment hurdles"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Behavioural biases in finance: roots, consequences, and evidence.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Anomalies or a theory?** The strongest criticism of behavioural finance comes from
@fama1998, who argued that the literature had produced a list of anomalies rather than
a theory: some studies find underreaction, others overreaction, and many anomalies
are sensitive to methodology. Behavioural researchers have responded with models that
derive both patterns from a few psychological assumptions, with out-of-sample tests
such as those of sentiment indices [@baker2006], and with individual trading data in
which biases can be observed directly [@odean1998; @barber2001]. Biases observed in
trading records have generally proved sturdier than return anomalies, many of which
have shrunk since publication [@mclean2016].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**GameStop, January 2021.** In late 2020 GameStop, a struggling video-game retailer,
was one of the most heavily shorted stocks in the US market, with reported short
interest exceeding the number of shares available for trading. Retail investors,
many coordinating on the Reddit forum r/wallstreetbets and trading through commission-free
apps, began buying the shares and call options. The price rose from under 20 dollars
at the start of January 2021 to a closing high above 300 dollars on 27 January.
Several hedge funds with short positions suffered large losses, and one, Melvin
Capital, received a multibillion-dollar capital infusion from other investment firms.
On 28 January several brokers restricted purchases of GameStop and other "meme
stocks", citing sharply higher collateral requirements at their clearinghouse. The
SEC staff report on the episode found that short covering accounted for only a small
part of the buying and that the rise was driven mainly by investors who were not
covering short positions [@sec2021].

The episode combines the chapter's theories. Social contagion and sentiment, see
[Social transmission](#social-transmission) (Section \@ref(social-transmission)) and [Conformity](#conformity) (Section \@ref(conformity)), produced
correlated noise trading. Short sellers faced unlimited potential losses and margin
calls, so betting against the rally was extremely risky even for investors convinced
that the price exceeded fundamental value, as @delong1990 and @shleifer1997 predict.
GameStop then sold new shares at the elevated price later in 2021, the market timing
of @baker2002.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Retail investors who receive more push notifications trade more frequently and
  earn lower risk-adjusted net returns, an effect moderated by financial literacy.
- *H2.* Firms issue more equity and conduct fewer repurchases when sentiment for their
  industry is high, controlling for investment opportunities.

**Measures.** Turnover, realised gains and losses (PGR and PLR), sentiment indices,
social media attention, short interest, retail order flow, issuance and repurchase
activity.

**Designs.** Account-level brokerage data, field experiments on information
presentation, natural experiments from app feature rollouts, panel regressions of
issuance on sentiment, laboratory asset markets.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Naming a bias instead of testing it.** It is easy to label any pattern in returns
with a bias after the fact. A credible behavioural finance study derives a prediction
from a specific psychological mechanism, shows that the mechanism operates in the
population studied, and rules out risk-based and institutional explanations,
ideally with a test where the behavioural and rational accounts predict different
outcomes.
:::

## Chapter Summary {#finance-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- **Portfolio theory**: risk is a property of portfolios. Diversification removes
  idiosyncratic risk [@markowitz1952; @tobin1958].
- The **CAPM** prices only systematic risk through beta [@sharpe1964; @lintner1965].
  Its empirical failures led to multifactor models [@fama1992; @fama1993].
- The **efficient market hypothesis** holds that prices reflect available information
  [@fama1970]. Index funds rest on its most robust implication [@sharpe1991], while
  excess volatility shows that prices need not equal fundamental value [@shiller1981].
- The **Modigliani-Miller theorems** make financing irrelevant in perfect markets
  [@modigliani1958], turning every friction, starting with taxes [@modigliani1963],
  into a candidate theory of capital structure.
- The **trade-off** and **pecking order** theories explain leverage through tax
  shields and distress costs, and through information asymmetry, respectively. Neither
  fully fits the data [@myers1984a; @shyamsunder1999; @frank2003].
- **Free cash flow theory** explains why debt, payouts, and takeovers can create value
  in mature, cash-rich firms [@jensen1986].
- **Limits to arbitrage** explain why mispricing persists: arbitrage is risky and
  capital is impatient [@delong1990; @shleifer1997].
- **Behavioral finance** combines limits to arbitrage with investor psychology to
  explain trading, anomalies, and corporate financing choices [@barberis2003].
:::

Table \@ref(tab:tab-fin-summary) presents the comparison of the chapter's theories.

```{r tab-fin-summary}

  "Efficient market hypothesis", "Competition among informed traders", "No predictable abnormal returns", "Anomalies, excess volatility", "Index funds, event studies",
  "Modigliani-Miller", "Arbitrage and homemade leverage", "Financing irrelevant in perfect markets", "Assumptions rarely hold", "Benchmark for financing decisions",
  "Trade-off and pecking order", "Taxes versus distress, information asymmetry", "Target leverage or financing hierarchy", "Persistence, market timing", "Leverage and issuance policy",
  "Free cash flow theory", "Agency costs of surplus cash", "Debt and payouts discipline managers", "Precautionary cash holdings", "Payout policy, buyouts",
  "Limits to arbitrage", "Risky, capital-constrained arbitrage", "Mispricing persists where arbitrage is hard", "Ex post flexibility", "Risk management, hedge fund design",
  "Behavioral finance", "Investor biases plus limits to arbitrage", "Sentiment and bias-driven mispricing", "Many anomalies, few unified models", "Product design, market timing"
) |>

## Discussion Questions {#finance-questions}

1. Many founders and executives hold most of their wealth in a single firm. Using
   agency theory and portfolio theory, explain when such concentration is efficient
   for the firm even if it is costly for the individual.
2. The CAPM fails many empirical tests yet remains the most common method for
   estimating the cost of equity. Is this a failure of practice or a defensible choice?
3. Design an event study of a sustainability announcement. Which form of market
   efficiency must hold for your estimate to be meaningful?
4. A CFO argues that because debt is cheaper than equity, more leverage lowers the
   cost of capital. Evaluate the argument with the Modigliani-Miller propositions and
   the trade-off theory.
5. Large technology firms hold very large cash balances. Develop competing hypotheses
   from free cash flow and pecking order theory, and describe data that could
   distinguish them.
6. Using the GameStop episode, explain why short sellers who believed the stock was
   overvalued might rationally have closed their positions. What does this imply for
   price efficiency during episodes of extreme sentiment?

## Further Reading {#finance-reading}

- @markowitz1952: the short paper that founded modern portfolio theory and remains a
  model of clear argument.
- @fama2004: an accessible review of the CAPM's logic, its empirical record, and why
  its failures matter for practice.
- @fama1970: the classic synthesis of market efficiency, with the three forms and the
  joint hypothesis problem.
- @myers2001: a lucid survey of capital structure theories from Modigliani-Miller
  through the trade-off and pecking order debates.
- @jensen1986: a compact statement of free cash flow theory that shaped two decades of
  research on payouts and takeovers.
- @shleifer1997: the paper that explains why arbitrage fails when it is most needed,
  vindicated by the LTCM crisis a year later.
- @barberis2003: the standard survey of behavioural finance, organised around limits
  to arbitrage and investor psychology.
- @french2008: a careful accounting of what investors spend trying to beat the market,
  essential background for the index fund debate.
